about: Authored countries a generated world may hold, each where its requirements fit: beyond a march on the side named, of a country of one of the terrains named. The first march a company reaches where one fits leads into it instead of a country drawn from the seed; each is placed once in a world (src/world/frontier.ts). Of the countries among one kind (the independent adventures), a world holds only the one its seed chooses. Each says what the folk of the first region say of it (rumour, with {keeper} whoever keeps travellers in the town it is asked in), what it is asked about (topic), what the company knows of it once told (heard), and, for one whose news is posted, the notice every town of the first region has nailed up (notice); and, for one that says when it is seen through, how the talk goes there after and what whoever keeps travellers says to the company come back from it (after).

countries.name: Merrowdale
countries.rumour: 'Up the north road there is Merrowdale,' says {keeper}. 'There is a long ridge across the head of the dale, and they say a giant king is buried under it. Something tall walks the crest at night. The steward has posted forty crowns to have it laid.'
countries.heard: Up the north road lies Merrowdale, where a giant king is said to be buried under the long ridge, and something tall walks its crest at night.

notice.name: a notice from Merrowdale
notice.text: A notice in a clerk's hand, carried down from Merrowdale and nailed up where travellers will see it: WHOEVER LAYS THE MOWER THAT WALKS THE LONG MAN SHALL HAVE FORTY CROWNS OF THE STEWARD. A. VENN, FOR THE LORD. Under it someone has written: up the north road, over the march, three days at most.
notice.talk: A notice from Merrowdale is nailed up where travellers will see it, and half the talk is of the forty crowns it offers and the other half of why nobody has gone.

after.talk: A notice from Merrowdale still hangs where travellers will see it, curling at the corners. Nobody talks of the forty crowns now: the word down the north road is that the Long Man is quiet.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, all of it, without a word. 'There was word of it already,' {keeper} says then. 'Off the north road: the thing on the ridge is quiet, and nobody up there talks of forty crowns any more. Nobody said who.' {keeper} looks at you a while longer, then reaches up and takes the notice from Merrowdale down, and puts it on the fire.

countries.name: Thrume
countries.rumour: 'East over the march, under the fells, there is a salt town, Saltgrave,' says {keeper}. 'People pay to sleep there, and some of them do not come home. And the giants have come down off the mountain, they say, for the first time anyone remembers.'
countries.heard: East over the march lies Saltgrave, a salt town under the fells, where people pay to sleep and some do not come home, and the giants have come down off the mountain.

countries.name: the Strewnfield
countries.topic: the room of glass in the Strewnfield
countries.rumour: 'South, in the Strewnfield,' says {keeper}, 'a room of glass fell into a barley field by Cobble Ring. It grows, they say, wherever nobody is watching it. They sit up with it all night on stools.'
countries.heard: South over the march lies the Strewnfield, where a room of glass fell into a barley field by Cobble Ring, and grows wherever nobody watches it.

countries.name: the Corrow
countries.rumour: 'West of here is the Corrow,' says {keeper}. 'There is a mountain hangs over it in the sky, on a chain, and they say it is drifting. And there is a well there nobody has been to the bottom of.'
countries.heard: West over the march lies the Corrow, where a mountain hangs in the sky on a chain, drifting, over a well nobody has been to the bottom of.

countries.name: the Ghessil Uplands
countries.rumour: 'West, up on the Ghessil Uplands,' says {keeper}, 'there is a light lies on the glass that slows whatever drinks it. There are people standing in it, they say, that went in last autumn and are standing there yet, alive.'
countries.heard: West over the march lie the Ghessil Uplands, where a light on the glass slows whatever drinks it, and people stand in it alive since last autumn.

countries.name: the Bowl of Ammerlin
countries.rumour: 'South over the march there's a city down the inside of a crater, Ammerlin,' says {keeper}. 'Their lake's been going down three years, and nobody there will believe anybody else about why. So they've sent out for someone from outside to measure it, and put their name to the answer. The Office of Measures pays, if you can count.'
countries.heard: South over the march lies the Bowl of Ammerlin, a city down the inside of a crater, whose lake has been falling for three years; its Office of Measures wants someone from outside to measure it and say why.

countries.name: the Ossel delta
countries.rumour: 'Down the east road, where the marsh meets the sea, there's Tessary on the Ossel,' says {keeper}. 'Their legions came home from the war a week back, and they say some of the soldiers are getting up in the night and walking into the sea. Barefoot, in step, eyes open. An eel-wife there has put up a notice: she'll give her savings to anyone who can tell her where her boy went.'
countries.heard: East over the march lies Tessary on the Ossel, where the legions have come home from the war and some of the soldiers walk into the sea at night; an eel-wife there offers her savings for news of her son.

countries.name: the vale of the Arle
countries.rumour: 'West over the march, where the Ise falls into the Arle, there's Pentrice,' says {keeper}. 'A minster town, very grand, where they license every word said on a stage and fine you for the rest. This week it's their Midsummer Trial: three companies of players, three nights in a round playhouse over the river, and the best of them given a house of its own for ever.' {keeper} grins. 'They say old Absalom Gosse is going back for it, after forty years. They banned him from the walls the last time. He started a riot.'
countries.heard: West over the march lies Pentrice, a minster town that licenses every word said on a stage; this week it holds its Midsummer Trial, three companies of players for three nights, and Absalom Gosse's company is going back after forty years' banishment.

notice.name: a playbill of the Midsummer Trial
notice.text: A bill in red and black, much handled and rained on: THE MIDSUMMER TRIAL AT THE WHEEL OF PENTRICE. THREE COMPANIES OF PLAYERS. THREE NIGHTS. THE PATENT OF THE WHEEL TO BE GIVEN BY THE BENCH. BY LEAVE OF THE OFFICE OF PLAIN SPEECH. Under it someone has written in pencil: west road, over the march, a day; and drawn a bear.
notice.talk: A playbill of the Midsummer Trial at Pentrice is nailed up where travellers will see it, and half the talk is of who will win the Patent and the other half of whether old Gosse will be let in at the gate.

after.talk: A playbill of the Midsummer Trial at Pentrice still hangs where travellers will see it, curling at the corners. The Trial is over: the word off the west road is all of what happened on the last night, and nobody tells it the same way twice.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, all of it, from the Westgate to the verdict, and laughs in the right places, and once does not laugh at all. 'We heard some of it,' {keeper} says then. 'Off the west road. Not the half of it.' {keeper} reaches up and takes down the playbill of the Midsummer Trial, and folds it, and puts it behind the bar, not on the fire.
